title: hardware-specific-tuning-a100-h100-l4-mi300
content:
Purpose:
This is a working notes doc for hardware-specific tuning of Redwood's serving runtime. Focus: A100, H100, L4 (inference-class), and AMD MI300. Topics: clocking & power limits, kernel selection/flags, scheduler hints, and KV-cache placement/eviction tradeoffs.

Status and context:
- Draft, iterative. Mostly capture observed tuning knobs and recommended defaults for Dedicated / Private deployments.
- Intended audience: eng-serving-runtime, release-engineering, SRE.
- Not a final playbook; will convert to runbooks after validation.

High-level goals (for tuning):
- Stable tail latency (99.9/99.99) for single-request and low-batch scenarios.
- Maximize throughput tokens/sec for batched workloads within power/TDP constraints.
- Keep KV-cache hits off HBM where possible to avoid eviction storms during peaks.

Hardware overview (quick):
- A100 (40/80GB HBM): good memory capacity, predictable clocks. Supports MIG on certain SKUs.
- H100 (80GB SXM / PCIe variants): higher peak FLOPS, stronger mixed-precision perf, more aggressive boost behavior.
- L4 (inference-optimized, ~24GB GDDR): lower-power, good INT8/FP16 perf for smaller models and cost-sensitive routes.
- MI300 (AMD CDNA3, large HBM pools, ROCm stack): strong memory bandwidth; different driver toolchain (ROCm/RSMI).

Clocking & power control recommendations (per-GPU):
- A100:
  - Set persistent clocks for inference processes when latency predictability is required. Use NVIDIA nvidia-smi -ac/persistence-mode + nvidia-smi -pl to set a stable power envelope.
  - Default power limit suggestion: 250W–300W for 40GB PCIe variants; 350W–400W for SXM 80GB depending on OEM. Tune based on thermal headroom.
  - Disable turbo/auto boost at system level if rack-level thermal variability causes jitter.

- H100:
  - H100 has more dynamic boost; prefer fixed clocks in latency-critical pools. Use nvidia-smi applications clocks or the RMM/driver hooks we expose.
  - Power limits: start at 350W for constrained racks, 450W for high-performance SXM deployments. Monitor sustained TGP and throttling.
  - Watch PCIe vs SXM differences: PCIe variants often hit power walls sooner — prefer lower clock targets.

- L4:
  - Default to TDP-limited mode: L4 is designed for lower power, so keep power limit in 75W–150W range depending on model density.
  - Favor frequency scaling for cost/perf: allow turbo only for cold-starts; otherwise keep a steady mid-level clock to save power and reduce noise.

- MI300 (AMD):
  - Use rocm-smi for clock and power tuning. Typical power limits vary widely by OEM; start conservative.
  - Ensure ROCm versions are pinned; driver/kernel mismatches cause large perf regressions.
  - Thermal and power telemetry is less granular than NVIDIA in some setups — add extra margin.

Common knobs and rationale:
- Persistent clocks vs auto: persistent (fixed) clocks reduce tail jitter at the cost of higher baseline power. Prefer for latency SLOs.
- Power capping: reduces throttling and overheating events that cause long tails. Set per-card power limit and monitor via telemetry.
- ECC: disable in private envs where acceptable to get small perf gains. Keep ECC enabled for customer workloads requiring data integrity.

Kernel tuning and compilation notes:
- CUDA kernels (A100/H100/L4):
  - Build kernels with cuda_arch flags matching SM versions of the fleet. Keep multiple tuned build variants (sm_80, sm_90, sm_86) and load the best match at runtime.
  - Use fusible kernels for attention/feed-forward where possible to reduce memory traffic.
  - For H100, target PTX for side-by-side launch to leverage new tensor core shapes and sparse support.
  - Use flags to enable TensorFloat32 or TF32 fallback per-model policy.

- ROCm kernels (MI300):
  - Build ROCm/HIP kernels with gfx1030/1031 targets (confirm exact GCN/GFX name for MI300 SKU).
  - Validate MIOpen convolution/tensor ops for correctness with our quantization codepath.
  - Keep a separate ROCm build matrix in CI.

Scheduler & placement hints (runtime-level):
- Scheduler goals: co-locate many small requests on L4-like cards; pin long KV-cache-resident models to high-memory cards (A100 80GB / MI300).
- Runtime should expose hints: "latency-critical", "throughput-batch", "kv-heavy", "memory-resident". Use these to pick model->GPU mapping and power profile.
- CPU affinity / NUMA: pin host threads that feed a GPU to the same NUMA node. Use hugepages for large model loads to reduce TLB misses.
- MPS / Multi-tenant: CUDA MPS can increase utilization for many small contexts, but it can interfere with per-request isolation and cause noisy-neighbor tail spikes. Use in dedicated low-isolation pools only.

KV-cache considerations (HBM vs host memory):
- Primary objective: keep KV-cache in HBM for hot keys to avoid PCIe/DDR round trips. Secondary: have a fallback host-backed reserve that can be paged in.
- A100/H100: HBM capacity matters. For models with large KV per-token (long-context models), prefer 80GB SKUs or MI300 where HBM > working set.
- L4: small HBM/GDDR -> better for short-context and smaller caching strategies; avoid trying to shove large KV caches here.
- MI300: large HBM is beneficial, but ROCm and host DMA semantics differ; benchmark our KV write/read path under MI300 to rule out unexpected stalls.

KV cache eviction policy suggestions:
- LRU with size thresholds tuned per-GPU type; don't aggressively evict on slight oversubscription — prefer batching spill to host.
- Prefetch hot prefixes: for streaming workloads, prefetch next N tokens into HBM when requester pattern is consistent.
- Eviction hysteresis: require a consistent pressure signal for > X seconds before aggressive eviction to avoid oscillation under bursty traffic.

Telemetry & metrics to collect for tuning feedback:
- Per-GPU: sm_util, mem_util, power_draw, clock_current, temp, avoid_count (throttling), ECC_errors.
- Per-model/per-route: tokens/sec, 50/95/99/99.9/99.99 latency, KV-cache hit rate, HBM occupancy fraction.
- Track scheduled vs actual: queue length per worker, scheduling latency, model load/unload times.

Benchmark plan (minimal):
1) Baseline: run perf harness (single-stream, batch sizes 1..64) across empty and loaded HBM states. Record tail latencies.
2) Power sweep: for each card type run at candidate power limits (e.g., -10%, 0%, +10% of nominal) and measure perf and tail.
3) Clocking modes: auto vs persistent at several clock targets.
4) KV stress: simulate many long-context clients to fill HBM and measure eviction behavior and latency impact.
5) ROCm-specific: run same flow on MI300 with ROCm pinned versions.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Validate exact SM/architecture targets for all SKUs in our fleet (inventory mismatch has caused bad PTX fallsbacks).
- Test MIG behavior on A100/H100 SKUs we plan to partition. How does KV cache isolation look across MIG slices?
- MI300: confirm driver/ROCm SMI telemetry naming and any OEM-specific quirks.
- Decide default power limits per fleet cluster and codify as config in cluster profiles.
- Perf regression guardrails in CI for kernel builds (esp. TF32/FP16 fused kernels).

Runbook snippets (for SRE):
- If tail latency climbs after hardware swap, check: power limit/persistence-mode, temperature throttling, driver version, and whether the runtime loaded correct kernel variant.
- If KV-hit-rate drops: check HBM occupancy, GC/eviction logs, and swap activity on host.

Notes & references:
- Keep a matrix mapping node SKU -> recommended power/pll/clock profile in repo (TODO: add as JSON under infra/host-profiles).
- Link to perf harness: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-harness (see perf/experiments/hardware-tuning).

Quick checklist for validation run (engineering):
- [ ] Inventory: export exact GPU model/revision for target cluster.
- [ ] Build: prepare CUDA/ROCm builds for target archs.
- [ ] Deploy: baseline driver + telemetry on canary nodes.
- [ ] Measure: run benchmark plan and store metrics in perf DB.
- [ ] Iterate: adjust power/clocks and re-run.

Appendix: example nvidia-smi commands (examples to standardize):
- persistence: sudo nvidia-smi -pm 1
- set application clocks: sudo nvidia-smi -ac <memClock,graphicsClock>
- set power limit: sudo nvidia-smi -pl 350
- query telemetry: nvidia-smi --query-gpu=index,name,utilization.gpu,utilization.memory,temperature.gpu,power.draw --format=csv

Example ROCm snippets (MI300):
- show clocks/power: sudo rocm-smi --showclocks --showpower
- set power cap: sudo rocm-smi --setpoweroverdrive <value> (OEM-specific)
